back: The smallest element of a bitmap image; each pixel is stored as a binary colour value.
The number of bits used for the colour of each pixel; n bits give 2^n colours.
The number of pixels in an image, width × height.
File size (bits) = width × height × colour depth. ÷ 8 for bytes, ÷ 1024 for KiB, ÷ 1024 again for MiB. Add the header if its size is given.

front: Effect of increasing resolution or colour depth
back: Better quality (more detail, more colours) but a larger file.
An image stored as a drawing list of objects (lines, shapes, text) and their properties.

front: Contents of a bitmap file header
back: Information about the image such as the file type, width, height and colour depth.
Bitmap for photographs and scans. Vector for logos, diagrams and maps that must scale without loss of quality.

front: Why do bitmaps lose quality when enlarged?
back: They have a fixed number of pixels, which become visible as blocks. Vector shapes are recalculated at the new size.
